title: fetch & HTTP client
lede: The WHATWG fetch client — fetch(), Response, Request, Headers — over libcurl, non-blocking under the event loop. The defining divergence from standard fetch: the response body accessors (.text()/.json()/.arrayBuffer()) are synchronous, returning the value directly rather than a Promise (awaiting them is a harmless no-op). Response headers can't be read yet. WebSocket, EventSource, and XMLHttpRequest are separate Networking surfaces, documented elsewhere.

entries.name: fetch(url, init?)
entries.signature: fetch(url: string | Request, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response>
entries.description: Issues an HTTP request and resolves when the response headers arrive; the body is read lazily. Genuinely non-blocking — awaited inside an http.listen handler it yields to the event loop, so a slow upstream call doesn't stall other connections. A network-level failure (DNS, connection refused, TLS, timeout) throws; a non-2xx HTTP status still resolves normally — .ok distinguishes it, matching real fetch.

params.name: url
params.desc: The target URL, or a Request object as the sole argument.

params.name: init?
params.desc: Any value with a subset of method: string / headers: Map<string,string> | Headers / body: string.

entries.snippet:
const r = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/get')
console.log(r.status, r.ok)   // 200 true
differences: Setting a `body` without an explicit `method` sends it as `POST` (libcurl's `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` implies `POST` unless overridden); an explicit `method` always wins over that default.
A fetch carrying an `AbortSignal` resolves at completion, not when headers arrive.

entries.name: Response.status / .ok
entries.signature: readonly status: number; readonly ok: boolean
entries.description: The HTTP status code, and whether it is in the 2xx range. A non-2xx response still resolves — check .ok rather than relying on fetch to throw.
entries.snippet:
const missing = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/status/404')
console.log(missing.status, missing.ok)   // 404 false

entries.name: Response.text()
entries.description: Reads the body to completion and returns it as a string. Both call styles work: const s = r.text() and await r.text() (awaiting a non-thenable is identity).
entries.snippet:
const r = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/get')
const body: string = r.text()
differences: **Synchronous** — returns `string` directly, not the `Promise<string>` real WHATWG fetch returns.
The result is a null-terminated string: a binary body with an embedded null byte truncates at the first one — use `.arrayBuffer()` for binary.
`.text()` after consuming `.body` returns `""` instead of the spec's already-disturbed `TypeError`.

entries.name: Response.json()
entries.description: Reads and parses the body as JSON, projecting it into a declared type. Reuses JSON.parse's machinery — validates the body (a non-JSON body throws a catchable SyntaxError) and projects nested objects, array/object-array fields, and top-level T[].

returns.desc: The parsed value, projected to the annotated type.

entries.snippet:
interface Ip { origin: string }
const info: Ip = (await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8765/ip')).json()
differences: **Synchronous** — returns the parsed value directly, not `Promise<any>`.
Only `any`/`unknown` dynamic shapes are unsupported; every statically-typed shape projects.
Same embedded-null truncation as `.text()` — the body is read as a null-terminated string.

entries.name: Response.arrayBuffer()
entries.description: Reads the body to completion and returns it as an ArrayBuffer, carrying the real byte count and coming back whole regardless of content. The binary-safe body accessor — use it for any body that may contain null bytes.

returns.desc: The complete response body as bytes.

entries.name: Response.body
entries.description: A real ReadableStream<Uint8Array> fed incrementally from libcurl's write callback with backpressure via curl pause/unpause. On an already-completed transfer it replays the buffered bytes as one chunk.
differences: Reading `.text()` after consuming `.body` returns `""` rather than the spec's already-disturbed `TypeError`; `Object.keys`/JSON of a Response expose an internal `__kml_pending` field.

entries.name: Response headers
entries.description: Reading response headers is not supported — no HEADERFUNCTION capture exists in this codebase yet. There is no .headers accessor on a Response, and XMLHttpRequest's .getResponseHeader()/.getAllResponseHeaders() are absent for the same reason. Request-side headers work fully.

entries.name: new Request(url, init?)
entries.signature: new Request(url: string, init?: RequestInit): Request
entries.description: A real Request class bundling a URL with method/headers/body — all readable directly (.url/.method/.headers/.body). method defaults to "GET", headers to an empty Headers, body to null. Works as fetch's sole argument, or supply a plain-object init to fetch directly.

entries.name: new Headers()
entries.description: A case-insensitive (lowercased-key) header bag. get/set/has/delete behave like Map<string,string>'s own — because storage-wise it is one. A real Headers instance is accepted anywhere fetch takes headers, alongside a plain Map<string,string>.

entries.name: Headers.append(name, value)
entries.description: Adds a header value, combining with a comma if name is already present instead of overwriting — the one behavior that distinguishes it from .set().
